title: Our Old Self Crucified with Christ
english: …Christ [died] according to the flesh, so that he might undo the sin of the world. We, however, do not die according to the flesh—how could we?—but to sin, as it is written (Romans 6:2); that is, we render sin idle and ineffective in ourselves by putting to death “the members that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed” (Colossians 3:5). We have been united, then, not merely with Christ’s death according to the flesh, but with the likeness of his death. And this would be understood as dying for sin, and not for his own sin—far from it! For God is blameless and utterly far from being able to do wrong. Rather, as I said, it was for the sin of the world: “For the death he died to sin, he died once for all” (Romans 6:10). So we have been united with him in the likeness of his death (Romans 6:5). And we shall certainly be united with him and share the same form in his resurrection as well, for we shall live in Christ. The flesh will come back to life, and we shall also live in another way, having dedicated our own souls to him and being transformed toward holiness and into a glorious way of life in the Holy Spirit.

“Knowing this, that our old self…,” and so on (Romans 6:6). Who is our old self, what is the body of sin that is done away with, and in what way was it crucified with Christ? We must look into this closely. Some will perhaps suppose that the earthly flesh is called the body of sin because it was given to the human soul by way of punishment, since the soul had sinned even before there were bodies; for that is how some think and speak. But since this opinion belongs to the Greeks, let us thrust it away as untrue.

By “body of sin” and “our old self,” then, he means the earthly body, which, from the old condition in Adam, must waste away into corruption; for we were condemned in him, the first man. Besides this, it is also sick with the love of pleasure, for that is how the flesh is by nature, because of its inborn impulses. How, then, was it crucified with Christ? The Only-begotten became man and clothed himself with the earthly flesh, which, as I said, had fallen sick with death because of the old condition in Adam, and which carried within itself, as if in labour, the tendency to be sharpened toward sin by its inborn impulses.

Yet the law of sin lies still in the holy and all-pure flesh of Christ. We certainly do not say that the more unseemly of the human passions were stirred in him, except those whose movement is blameless—I mean hunger and thirst and weariness, and whatever else the law of nature has kept free of blame even in us. Still, even though the law of sin was not stirred in Christ, because it was lulled to sleep by the power and working of the Word who carried out the dispensation, yet when the nature of the flesh is examined by itself, even if it is considered as it is in Christ, we shall find that it is no different from ours. So we were crucified with him when his flesh was crucified, flesh that held, as it were, the whole nature within itself; just as…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: the verb ἀπέθανε stands at the end of u03-open. '[died]' is bracketed as carried over from there; the leading ellipsis marks the join.
Ends mid-sentence at καθάπερ; u03-rem-mid continues ἀμέλει καὶ ἐν Ἀδάμ. The closing ellipsis marks the break.

οὐχὶ δὴ μόνον τῷ κατὰ σάρκα θανάτῳ Χριστοῦ: rendered literally 'not merely with Christ's death according to the flesh'. Cyril has just said that we do not die according to the flesh; μόνον may be a slip in the printed text, but nothing is changed.
ἵνα λύσῃ τοῦ κόσμου τὴν ἁμαρτίαν: possible echo of John 1:29 (τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου), but the verb differs; left uncited as uncertain.
ὁ τῆς ἁμαρτίας νόμος ('the law of sin') is Pauline language (Romans 7:23, 8:2) used as a term, not a quotation; not cited inline.

Ἑλλήνων ... τὴν δόξαν: the view that souls sinned before bodies and were given flesh as punishment; Cyril calls it the opinion of 'the Greeks' (pagan philosophy) and does not name anyone. No name is added.
παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος rendered 'old self' (modern standard for Romans 6:6); παλαιότης τῆς ἐν Ἀδάμ rendered 'the old condition in Adam'.
τοῦ οἰκονομοῦντος Λόγου rendered 'the Word who carried out the dispensation', as in 'the dispensation in the flesh' in u02-rem-early.
PG column numbers 191 and 192 and the page number 7 in the copy-text are dropped from the reading text.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u03 rem early

title: The Body of Sin Done Away
english: …just as in Adam too, when he came under the curse, the whole of human nature fell sick with that curse.
So too we are said to have been raised with Christ and to be seated with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6).
For even though Emmanuel is above us as God, yet since he became like us as one of us, he has been raised and sits beside God the Father.
So our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6), for through the resurrection the power of that ancient curse has been broken.

The body of sin has also been done away with (Romans 6:6). This does not mean the flesh itself, but the inborn savagery of the impulses within it, which always drags the mind down toward what is more shameful and sinks it, as it were, into the mud and marshes of earthier pleasures.

That this too has been accomplished for human nature in Christ, who could doubt, when Paul says plainly, “For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3)?

Do you see, then, how the body of sin has been done away with? For the sting of sin has been condemned in the flesh. It was put to death first in Christ, and the grace has passed from him and through him to us as well.
“Or do you not know, brothers—for I am speaking to those who know the law…” (Romans 7:1).
Everywhere he shows that to seek to be under the law is dangerous.

He urges us rather to long for, and with our whole mind to thirst after, the grace that comes through faith, that is, justification in Christ. He firmly declared that the baptized have been buried with Christ (Romans 6:4), so that, having been put to death to sin, they might live to God in righteousness (Romans 6:11).

That is why he said, “So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its desires. Do not present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members to God as weapons of righteousness. For sin will no longer have dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:12–14).
See, then, how he commands them to leave the shadow of the law (Hebrews 10:1) and instead to take shelter under the grace that is in Christ.

Yet the Spirit-bearer was well aware that some would surely say, or at least reason to themselves, that in that case the fathers had strayed from the straight road and from life, that the law had done them no good, and that the glories of their way of life had somehow already come to nothing.
For if it is absurd to seek to be under the law, and this was the aim of life for the people of old, how could it not be true to say that they missed what was fitting?

So he who has Christ within him takes up the contest. He skilfully gives the impression that he wishes to speak on behalf of those who lived under the law, but in many ways he turns the argument toward the view that, when the time calls to faith, one must not be too eager to linger over the ancient customs.
This is why he says, “Or do you not know, brothers, for I am speaking to those who know the law, that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives?” (Romans 7:1).
This is a general rule, holding both for…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The row opens mid-sentence: καθάπερ closes the previous row (u03-rem-early), so the English opens with an ellipsis. It also ends mid-sentence (ὅρος οὗτος γενικὸς κατά τε νόμου); the sentence continues in u03-rem-close.
παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος rendered “old self” for readability; Cyril means the earthly body bearing the ancient corruption from Adam (see u03-rem-early).
κέντρον τῆς ἁμαρτίας: “sting of sin”; a possible echo of 1 Corinthians 15:56, not cited inline because the wording differs.
Romans 8:3 kept in its elliptical Greek shape (“what was impossible for the law … God … condemned sin”) without supplying “God did”.
ὅπλα rendered “weapons” (Romans 6:13).
πνευματοφόρος (“the Spirit-bearer”) is Paul; Spirit capitalised as the Holy Spirit.
ὑποτρέχειν τὴν ἐν Χριστῷ χάριν: “take shelter under” the grace, keeping the image of running under cover set against the law’s shadow.
Possible echo of Genesis 3:17 (the curse in Adam) not cited inline; Cyril does not quote it.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u03 rem mid

title: Dead to the Law
english: …every law and for those who are under law.
For laws define, for all who live under the sceptres of kings, what must be done and what must not; but they have force only among those who are still alive.

If someone who is under law departs from life in the body, he has put off, together with his life, the authority of the laws as well. For if he has ceased from wrongdoing, the law too will surely have nothing more to do with him.
It is true, then, that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives (Romans 7:1).
We must also say what the aim of the passage is. He brings two useful points into it.
We, he says, who have been buried with Christ through baptism (Romans 6:4), who have died to sin (Romans 6:2), have passed outside the authority of the law, for we have been remade for another life.
But those who lived before his coming, not yet having undergone the death that is understood in Christ, were still living to sin.
So the law ruled over them as over the living, just as a husband rules over his wife.

For as a married woman, while the man lawfully joined to her is still alive, cannot unite with another man without answering for it, yet if he dies, he says, she will be free of penalty even if she chooses to do this, since she does it lawfully (Romans 7:2–3), in the same way, I think, those who did not yet have the deadening of sin in Christ, but were living, as it were, in sin, were rightly under law as well; for the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives.

But those who have already come under the grace that is in Christ, through which they have died to sin and been put to death to the flesh, that is, to the passions of the flesh, may lead a life outside the law without blame, if they are no longer reckoned as people living in the world (Colossians 2:20).
For, as I said, they have been put to death through the body of Christ, and they died to the law (Romans 7:4), being justified through faith.
“For while we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work,” and so on (Romans 7:5).
By “flesh” he means the fleshly mind, as he says elsewhere too: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:8).
And yet who would deny that he gives such instructions to those he was initiating into the mystery as to people who had not left the body?
What he means to show must be examined closely.
When we lived in a fleshly way, he says, and the earthly mind ruled in us, then the passions of the flesh were at work in us through the law, to bear fruit for death (Romans 7:5).
“What then?” someone might say. “Were the passions of the flesh brought in through the law? Then how shall we clear the law of the charges against it?”
What do we say to this? The passions of the flesh were not stirred in us through the law. Rather, they are born from inborn pleasure and they plunder the weak mind.
He makes this plain to us when he says, “The flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other” (Galatians 5:17).
Here, leaving this aside, he says that the flesh is set in battle against the Spirit, with nothing placed between them.
So the passions of the flesh are not stirred in us through the law, but rather by nature; and, strange to say, they rise up against the will of the law, as he himself somewhere…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The row opens mid-sentence (παντὸς καὶ τῶν ὑπὸ νόμον completes ὅρος οὗτος γενικὸς κατά τε νόμου from u03-rem-mid) and ends mid-sentence at ὡς αὐτός που; the sentence continues in u04-open (φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος).
μετεστοιχειώμεθα: literally “re-elemented”; rendered “remade”.
ἐπιδημία: Christ’s coming (the Incarnation); rendered “his coming”.
κἂν εἰ ἕλοιτο τοῦτο δρᾶν ἐννόμως: the adverb ἐννόμως qualifies the remarriage; rendered “even if she chooses to do this, since she does it lawfully”.
εἰ μηκέτι χρηματίζουσιν ὡς ζῶντες ἐν κόσμῳ kept as a condition (“if they are no longer reckoned…”), and the optative ποιοῖντο ἄν as “may lead”.
οὐκ ἔξω γεγονόσι: the object (the flesh, i.e. bodily life) is implied; Cyril’s point is that Paul’s hearers were still in the body, so “flesh” in Romans 7:5 must mean the fleshly mind.

τοῦτο παρείς: rendered literally “leaving this aside”; the referent is probably the law (in Galatians 5:17 Paul sets flesh against Spirit without naming the law between them), but the English keeps the Greek's open pronoun rather than supplying it.

καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἀληθὲς … οὐκ ἔξω γεγονόσι: kept as a rhetorical question (“who would deny…?”); the implied thing not left is the bodily flesh, so the reading text says “the body” to keep Cyril's contrast with the fleshly mind clear.
πνεῦμα in Galatians 5:17 and the following sentence capitalised as the Holy Spirit, following the common reading of the verse.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u03 rem close
